summary.text:
Bedfordshire Fire and Rescue Authority's Treasury Management Annual Report for 2025/26 (10 pages) was taken by the Fire and Rescue Authority on 14 July 2026, from ACO G Chambers (Gavin Chambers), Assistant Chief Officer / FRA Treasurer, signed off alongside Chief Fire Officer Andrew Hopkinson on p10. This is the substantive treasury outturn — it carries the CFR schedule and prudential-indicator table (§3.1, p4), the treasury position at both year-ends (§4.1, p5), the debt maturity structure (§4.2, p6), the investment portfolio split (§4.2 second table, p6), the borrowing and investment outturn narrative (§§5–7) and the balance-sheet resources summary (§7.2, p10). The front sheet lists ‘Treasury Management Strategy 2025/26’ as Appendix 1 but it is not bundled in this PDF. No loan-by-loan schedule is printed; only totals.

The loan book reconciles cleanly on principal. Our file, searched under the exact bc-loans name ‘BEDFORDSHIRE FIRE & RESCUE AUTHORITY’ (a naming trap: ‘Bedfordshire Fire and Rescue’ returns no match — borrower uses ampersand and drops the ‘and’), holds two PWLB advances totalling £9,987,000 at a coupon-weighted 4.2218%, both MATURITY-profile. Paper §4.1 (p5) prints PWLB £9,987k at 4.27% with 32 years' average life at both 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026. Principal ties to the pound. Rate sits 5bp apart — 4.2218% rounds to 4.22% on a coupon-weighted basis, and the paper's 4.27% would round from 4.265–4.274%, so the gap is consistent either with rounding convention or with the paper using an effective-interest measure. Average life 31.05 years vs paper's 32 (rounding-up convention). The paper describes it as ‘the historical loan of £9.987m predominantly for the build of Dunstable Community Fire Station’; we hold this as two advances (PW492471 £6.3m at 4.10% maturing 2056; PW494762 £3.687m at 4.43% maturing 2058), likely two tranches drawn against the same project 18 months apart. Both sit in the 10-years-and-over maturity bucket, matching §4.2's 100%-in-10y+ position exactly.

The balance-sheet identity (CFR minus external borrowing minus OLTL equals internal borrowing) ties to the pound at all three year-ends printed in §3.1. At 31 March 2025: CFR £6,992k minus PWLB £9,987k minus OLTL £428k equals −£3,423k, and the paper's Under/(over) borrowing line prints (3,423). At 31 March 2026: £6,605k minus £9,987k minus £259k equals −£3,641k, matching (3,641). At 31 March 2027 (projected): £6,215k minus £9,987k minus £87k equals −£3,859k, matching (3,859). Three ties from three year-ends. The over-borrowed position deepens by £218k each year, driven entirely by MRP applied against CFR (~£387k in 2025/26, ~£390k in 2026/27) net of OLTL run-off; external PWLB is stationary at £9.987m throughout. §3.1 attributes the over-borrowed position to the legacy Dunstable loan and states it ‘will correct itself when the Authority makes material capital investment’, with estate investment options flagged for FRA discussion during 2026/27.

The Authority sits simultaneously over-borrowed at the balance-sheet identity level (£3.641m at 31.3.26) and as a net treasury investor at the cash level: £19.000m of investments against £9.987m of PWLB plus £0.259m of OLTL gives net cash of £8.754m — the opposite pattern from most councils we have read. §6.1 names the £19m of new/re-invested 2025/26 deposits and their maturities: £12.5m matured in May 2026, £4.5m matures July 2026, £2m in November 2026 — so as of today (15 August 2026) £17m of the £19m has already matured and been re-invested. Investment yield fell from 4.37% to 4.13% year on year, reflecting the three Bank Rate cuts (May, August, December 2025, 4.50% → 3.75%). Financing costs run at 0.52% of net revenue — small even by fire-authority standards. Total investment income £0.867m against a £0.745m budget.

Two testable observations. First, the two side-by-side forecast tables in §5.2 (p8). The February 2025 approval-time forecast has Bank Rate falling to 3.25% by March 2027 and holding; the newer Link Group forecast (May 2026, also printed) has Bank Rate holding at 3.75% for another year (through Sep 2027) and only then falling. Across the PWLB curve the two sit 40–80bp apart at every published maturity, uniformly higher on the newer view — 5-year PWLB by March 2027 goes from 4.20% to 4.90%, 25-year from 5.50% to 5.90%, 50-year from 5.30% to 5.70%. Bank Rate at year-end (3.75%) matched what both forecasts had for the near horizon (§5.2 narrative: ‘Bank Rate did peak at 3.75% as anticipated’); the long end did not fall as anticipated (‘the initial expectation of significant rate reductions across the whole curve did not transpire’).

Second, on the DMO's premature repayment curve dated 14 August 2026, our canonical engine prices both PWLB loans below par with a net indicative discount of £1,954,230, or 19.6% of principal. Paper §6.2 correctly states that rescheduling was not undertaken because ‘the approximate 1% differential between PWLB new borrowing rates and premature repayment rates made rescheduling unviable’ — that is the standard repay-and-reborrow test and our engine gives the same answer. It is a different test from repaying from reserves without reborrowing, which is at least numerically available given the over-borrowed position and the £19m of investments (of which £17m has matured by August). Recorded as an observation with full caveats; never as advice. The DMO's quote is the only binding one; no MRP or accounting treatment is modelled.

FRA precedent (Avon-era caution in the earlier extract) had been to decline drafting first-contact emails on FRA papers on the grounds of scale and fit. Devon and Somerset (mg280) and East Sussex (mg395) both drafted in the current session on the strength of exact reconciliations and substantive observations; Bedfordshire fits the same pattern — principal ties to the pound, balance-sheet identity ties three-for-three, and the two forecast tables give a genuine treasurer observation. A draft is prepared per the session's instruction; the FRA precedent and the address gap are flagged in reviewer notes. No email address is published for the Treasurer anywhere in the paper — only ACO G Chambers, 01234 845000 on the front sheet contact block — so an address is needed before send.

officer.body:
Dear Gavin,

Apologies for the cold email — PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're a small platform that carries PWLB rates at both fixings each working day, monthly local-authority-to-local-authority lending, every council and fire authority's PWLB loan book, and a lightweight academy for treasury officers. The data side is free and it will stay free. The one-page brochure is at pwlbtoday.com/brochure if it helps to circulate internally.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every authority in the country, so we can see how each authority's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. Below are some thoughts on your 14 July annual treasury report. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is short and clear, unusually so, and this is offered in that spirit rather than as a critique.

Your §4.1 gives the loan-book totals but not a loan-by-loan schedule, so this is where our file has something to add. Under the exact DMO borrower name 'BEDFORDSHIRE FIRE & RESCUE AUTHORITY' our file returns two PWLB advances — PW492471 for £6.300m at 4.10% maturing 30 September 2056, and PW494762 for £3.687m at 4.43% maturing 31 March 2058 — totalling £9,987,000 at a coupon-weighted 4.2218%. That matches your §4.1 total of £9.987m to the pound and your printed 4.27% within five basis points, which sits inside the rounding of a 4.22% coupon-weighted figure or is consistent with the paper using an effective-interest measure. Your §4.2 maturity table places 100% of the debt in the 10-year-and-over bucket, and both loans sit ~30 years out on our side too. Your §3.1 refers to 'the historical loan' for Dunstable Community Fire Station in the singular; we hold it as two advances 18 months apart, most likely drawn as two tranches against the same project.

The balance-sheet identity in §3.1 also ties clean: CFR minus external borrowing minus OLTL equals internal borrowing at all three year-ends printed. £6,992k − £9,987k − £428k = −£3,423k at 31.3.25 (you print (3,423)); £6,605k − £9,987k − £259k = −£3,641k at 31.3.26 (you print (3,641)); £6,215k − £9,987k − £87k = −£3,859k at 31.3.27 (you print (3,859)). Three ties from three year-ends. The over-borrowed position deepens by £218k each year, driven by MRP net of OLTL run-off, with external debt stationary at £9.987m throughout — which is what the two long-dated fixed maturities in our file would give.

What we can add against the two forecast tables in §5.2 is a straightforward market comparison. Your approval-time forecast (February 2025) has Bank Rate falling to 3.25% by March 2027 and holding, while the newer Link Group forecast (May 2026) has Bank Rate holding at 3.75% for another year before falling. Across the PWLB curve the two sit 40 to 80 basis points apart at every printed maturity, uniformly higher on the newer view — 5-year PWLB by March 2027 rises from 4.20% to 4.90%, 25-year from 5.50% to 5.90%, 50-year from 5.30% to 5.70%. Whether your next Estate capital investment is funded internally, from PWLB or from LA-to-LA borrowing, that upward drift is what any refinancing conversation is now priced against. Our /pwlb-activity page carries the daily rates at both fixings if it helps to keep the comparison live.

One observation with heavy caveats. On today's DMO premature repayment curve (notice 314/26 PM, 14 August 2026), our engine prices both loans below par with a net indicative discount of £1.95m — 19.6% of principal. Your §6.2 correctly states that rescheduling was not undertaken because the approximate 1% differential between new-borrowing and premature-repayment rates made rescheduling unviable, and on that repay-and-reborrow test our engine gives the same answer. The different test — repaying from reserves without reborrowing, given the over-borrowed position and the £19m of investments (of which £17m has already matured this year per §6.1) — is one we can price separately. This is indicative only; only the DMO can quote a binding figure. We model no MRP or accounting treatment, and whether any of it is worth doing turns on the estate-investment decisions §3.1 flags for FRA discussion during 2026/27, which sit outside our model. It is not a recommendation.

The academy is a paid product with three sessions that would fit what you have just presented: a walkthrough of the Liability Benchmark, a session on premature repayment and rescheduling arithmetic covering the not-reborrow frame above, and a Prudential and Treasury Code refresher pitched at fire-authority scale. Free account sign-up is at pwlbtoday.com/sign-up; the new-account discount runs until end of September.

If any of this lands, word of mouth is how we get in front of colleagues elsewhere — a mention to a peer treasurer in the region does more than any campaign we could run.
